newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson set to tell his story in court.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson set to tell his story in court.

text.p: O.J. Simpson, who took a verbal battering from plaintiffs' lawyers nearly two months ago, is expected to take the witness stand again in his civil trial on Friday to face gentler questioning from his own attorneys.

He had originally been called to give testimony on his own behalf last month, but the day he was scheduled to appear on the witness stand it was postponed because of a decision in another court in his child custody battle.

In that case, a judge in suburban Orange County awarded Simpson full custody of the two children he had with his slain ex-wife. His former in-laws wanted to keep their grandchildren, who had lived with them since just after their mother's murder.

Simpson was acquitted in criminal court in October 1995 in the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend, Ronald Goldman. He is now battling a wrongful-death civil lawsuit brought by the families of the victims.

The former American football star and TV personality, who never testified in his criminal trial, was called to the stand in November by the plaintiffs' lawyers, who sought to catch him in inconsistencies on his movements the night of the murders in June 1994.

During sometimes hostile questioning, Simpson stated emphatically that he never struck his ex-wife, but later testimony by his friend, Al Cowlings, contradicted that, and two other witnesses said they had seen Simpson hit Nicole Brown Simpson on separate occasions.
The defence chose not to question Simpson at the time but will do so starting on Friday, giving him the chance to explain once again what he was doing the night of the murders.

"The critical point will be when O.J. Simpson takes the stand," said CBS legal analyst Kristin Jeanette-Myers. "He has got lots to explain. This is his chance to clear up questions about domestic violence, cuts on his hands, the shoes and what he was doing that night."

The reference to shoes is one of the key unanswered questions in the case. FBI expert William Bodziak, who testified at both trials, said a bloody footprint at the murder scene, believed to be the killer's, was made by a distinctive size 12 Bruno Magli shoe.

Simpson said in a sworn deposition for his civil trial that he never owned such "ugly-ass" shoes, and Robert Groden, a photographic analyst called by the defence, branded a photograph of Simpson wearing Bruno Magli shoes a fake.

But photos by another photographer of Simpson apparently wearing the distinctive footwear at the same event were introduced at the trial on Monday. The defence, which has sought to show Simpson was framed and that evidence was planted, must now show that those photos too are fake.
In Thursday's testimony, a forensic expert said evidence in the case could have been contaminated by sloppy police work and that vital evidence was missed.

Henry Lee, chief criminalist for the state of Connecticut, told the jury via videotape that evidence was bagged and handled when still wet with blood and that police investigators failed to pick up blood drops and missed a footprint at the murder scene.

Simpson's lawyers have told Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki they will wrap up their case on Monday. The rebuttal phase will follow and then will come closing arguments, with the jury likely to start their deliberations before the end of the month.
